title: Scribe a full circle with spring dividers, keeping the point seated in the center-punch mark all the way round
instruction: Scribe the full circle for the hole on the blue steel plate with the dividers, centered on the punch mark, then stand the dividers back in the cork.
context: Machinists, tool and die makers and sheet-metal workers (O*NET 51-4041.00, 51-4111.00, 47-2211.00) lay out holes before drilling or cutting: they set one point of a pair of spring dividers in a center-punch mark, press lightly on the handle and swing the other leg a full turn so its point scribes the circle through the layout dye. The punch mark is all that holds the pivot leg, so it must stay seated under pressure the whole way round; if the point skates out mid-swing, the rest of the line comes out doubled or off-center and the layout is spoiled, since a scribed line in steel can't be rubbed out. Starting off the mark gives a circle with the wrong center, and stopping short leaves a gap. The dividers go back in their cork so the points stay sharp.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; the layout is the same in every trial. A mild steel plate, 13 x 11.5 cm and 6 mm thick, coated with blue layout dye, lies fixed on the table at x 20 to 33, y -15.5 to -4. Two bright scribed center lines, 9 cm long, cross on it at x 26, y -10, where there is a center-punch mark about 2 mm across: the center of a 60 mm hole to lay out. A dark cork block, 6 x 6 cm and 6 mm thick (its top level with the plate's), is fixed at x 23 to 29, y -24.5 to -18.5, 3 cm to the robot's right of the plate. A pair of 100 mm spring dividers (80 g), already set to a 30 mm radius, stands upright with both points stuck in the cork, its legs along x (points at x 24.5 and 27.5, y -21.5). The two steel legs meet a spring bow 9.6 cm up, with an adjusting screw and nut across them; on top is a black knurled handle 2.6 cm across and 2.4 cm tall (11.2 to 13.6 cm above the points, 20 g), centered between the legs, which slides 4 mm down its stem against a light spring (1.5 N at rest, 3.5 N fully down). The dividers can be lifted, carried and turned; they stay upright and fall back onto the steel or cork under their own weight when let go. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The points are down when within 0.5 mm of the steel. The pivot point is seated in the punch mark when the points are down and it drops within 0.5 mm of the mark's center (a lightly struck mark is about 2 mm across with a 90-degree cone); it stays seated until pushed 1.5 mm off (the mark's 1 mm rim plus 0.5 mm for the sim's play in the seated point), or until the dividers have turned 1 degree (0.5 mm at the scribing point, about the mark's depth) away from where the handle stopped being pressed at least 1.5 mm (2.25 N, a light fingertip press): unpressed, the scribing point's drag lifts the pivot out. The arc is the set of 0.1-degree sectors of the circle the scribing leg swept with the pivot seated (back and forth over the same sector counts once). Score 0, irreversibly, if either point ever moved more than 1 mm in all over the plate while down without the pivot seated: starting off the mark, skating out of it mid-swing, or dragging the dividers across the plate (a stray scratch that long shows plainly in layout dye and reads as a second line). Nothing counts while a tool point is within 3 cm of the handle's center (it is 2.6 cm across). Otherwise, at the end: 1.0 with at least 355 degrees scribed (a 5-degree gap is 2.6 mm on the 60 mm circle, about a saw kerf) and the dividers standing back in the cork (points down, both at least 3 mm inside its edges), both arms back home (each tool point within 3 cm of its start) and still for 1 s; 0.9 the same with the arms elsewhere; 0.75 at least 355 degrees scribed with the dividers left elsewhere; 0.5 at least 180 degrees scribed (half the circle, the least that is real progress); 0 otherwise, including doing nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 1.0. In a real trial, film from above, then check the plate under a loupe: one clean circle centered on the punch mark with no doubled or offset arc or scratch, the gap measured with a scale, and the dividers standing in the cork.
reset_notes: Stand the dividers back in the cork block, the handle over its center and the legs along x, set to a 30 mm radius. A scribed line can't be removed: use a fresh plate (or re-dye this one, scribe the center lines and punch the mark at the same place).
fidelity: The dividers are rigid and ride upright on joints (they can't tip), spread fixed at 30 mm; the handle is enlarged from about 8 mm to 2.6 cm for the gripper. The points don't cut: the seat in the mark is a condition on the joints that narrows the dividers' slides to 0.3 mm while in, and the line is drawn as dots (1.6 mm wide to show on camera) where the scribing point has been while down; the points' friction on the steel is damping.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2,400 steps: the right hand hovers and paws at the dividers in the cork, they never reach the plate); demo: 1.0 (success at step 905)
